title: A parity plot asks: does the cheap surrogate reproduce the expensive simulation on points it has not seen?
summary: Each point pairs the surrogate's estimate with the direct simulation of the same parameter set. Points on the diagonal agree. Training and testing points are drawn differently, and the legend states the largest percentage miss for each, so the picture checks both the fit and its generalization.

media.alt: Parity plot: response surface estimate on x, direct simulation on y, both from about 7.5 to 10. Open green training circles and filled black testing dots lie on a narrow diagonal band along the blue parity line; the legend gives maximum errors of 0.747 percent for testing and 0.691 percent for training.

read_the_figure.question: Is the response-surface approximation as accurate as needed to replace direct simulation inside an optimizer, including on data it was not fitted to?
read_the_figure.axes: x: the response-surface estimate of the output. y: the direct simulation of the same output at the same parameter set. Both axes are in the same units and have the same range, so the diagonal (the parity line) is exact agreement. Open green circles: training points (used to fit the surface). Filled black dots: testing points (held out). The legend gives, for each set, the maximum error in percent (and in one figure the mean error).
look_at: Distance from the diagonal: the vertical gap of a dot from the line is the surface's error at that point.
Compare the black dots with the green circles. Black dots as tightly on the line as the green ones means the surface generalizes; black dots scattering more means overfitting.

Look at the ends of the range. Errors are usually largest at the edges of the sampled region, where the polynomial is extrapolating its own behaviour; a few outlying green circles at one end are such points.
Compare the printed maximum errors with the scatter you see. A maximum is a worst case over many points, so the typical error is smaller.
The group's figures show the same plot for a fit with all parameters in the model and one with a reduced set, and for another data set with a wider scatter. Compare their legends side by side.
read_the_figure.proves: That on this sample the surface reproduces the simulation to within the printed worst-case percentage, for the points tested. It does not show the surface is valid everywhere: only inside the sampled region, and only as far as the test points cover it.
if_wrong: Dots curving away from the diagonal at the ends: the polynomial is too low in order for the shape of the response.
A cloud rather than a line: the surface misses much of the variation; the printed maximum error will be large.
Test points much worse than training points: overfitting, too many coefficients for the number of training runs.

A very tight line that spans a narrow range: the percentage errors are small relative to the value, but the spread of the outputs is small too. A tight parity plot over a narrow range is a weaker statement than over a wide one.
must_check: Both axes use the same range, so the parity line is at 45 degrees.
Training and testing points are shown separately and the test set was not used in the fit.
The error measure is defined (here a percentage of the value) and the output quantity has a name and unit; this figure shows only 'direct simulation' and 'response surface estimation' on the axes.
The number of training and testing points is stated; the figure does not state them.
Maximum error alone is not the whole story: a mean error or a root-mean-square error should accompany it.

terms.meaning: A fitted polynomial in the parameters that approximates the output of an expensive simulation. After fitting, it can be evaluated in microseconds.
A scatter of predicted against true values with the line y = x drawn. Distance from that line is the prediction error.
Training points are used to fit the coefficients; testing points are held back and used only to measure the error.
The largest percentage difference between estimate and simulation over a set of points: a worst case, not a typical error.
A fit using every parameter as an input, against one using a smaller set of combined or selected inputs. The reduced fit has fewer coefficients and needs fewer simulations to fit.
A fit that follows the training points' noise and so does worse on new points.

remember: On a parity plot the vertical distance from the diagonal is the error.
Judge the surrogate on the held-out dots, not the training circles.
A printed maximum is the worst case; the typical error is smaller.
A narrow output range makes any parity plot look tight.
A quadratic in n inputs has (n + 1)(n + 2) / 2 coefficients, so reducing the inputs cuts the sampling cost sharply.

understand.title: Why a surrogate at all
understand.text: An optimizer asks for the objective thousands of times. If every request is a full reaction-kinetics simulation, the search is expensive. A fitted polynomial is an inexpensive stand-in; the parity plot is the evidence that the stand-in is faithful.

understand.title: Full versus reduced
understand.text: The first two figures are the same data fitted with all parameters and with a reduced set. Their legends show that the reduced fit has errors of about the same size as the full one while using fewer inputs. That is the claim of the reduced parameterization: nearly the same accuracy at a fraction of the sampling cost.

understand.title: The third figure
understand.text: The third figure of the group has a wider cloud and larger maximum errors on the training set than on the test set, and its legend also gives mean errors that are close to zero. A near-zero mean with a large maximum means the errors are of both signs and a few points are far off. Note that this file is filed under a different caption in the project page; see the note below.

steps.title: A quadratic response surface
steps.tex: \hat y(x)=\beta_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i\le j\le n}\beta_{ij}\,x_i x_j
steps.note: Linear in the coefficients, so the coefficients are found by ordinary least squares from the training runs.

steps.title: Number of coefficients
steps.note: For n inputs. n = 5 gives 21 coefficients and n = 10 gives 66. At least that many training simulations are needed, and usually several times more.

steps.title: Least squares fit
steps.note: X holds the monomials evaluated at the training points. This is the normal equation, solved by a stable method in practice.

steps.title: The error shown in the legend
steps.note: The signed errors have a mean (which can be near zero when errors are of both signs) and a maximum of the absolute value.

steps.title: Why a narrow range flatters the plot
steps.note: The denominator is the spread of the outputs. For a given absolute error, a smaller spread lowers R squared; the same percentage error on a wider range looks tighter on the plot.

worked.title: Coefficients and the size of the miss
worked.problem: How many coefficients does a quadratic surface in n = 10 inputs have, versus n = 5? And what absolute miss is a 0.75 percent error on an output near 8.75 (the output values on the axes of the first figure run from about 7.8 to 9.6)?

solution.text: Absolute miss for a relative error of 0.75 percent.

worked.answer: 66 against 21 coefficients, so the reduced set needs about a third of the minimum number of runs; and a 0.75 percent error is a miss of about 0.07 in the axis units, small against an output range of about 1.8.

analyze.q: The reduced fit has about the same maximum errors as the full fit. List two reasons it might be as good, and one way it could be hiding a weakness.
analyze.hint: Parameters that matter little; a narrow test region; test points like the training points.

analyze.q: Training maximum error is larger than the testing maximum error in one figure. Is that evidence against overfitting?
analyze.hint: The test set may be smaller, so its maximum is smaller by chance.

analyze.q: Why can a near-zero mean error coexist with a large maximum error?

evaluate.q: Would you accept this surrogate inside an optimizer? What would you check at the boundaries of the parameter box?
evaluate.hint: The optimizer will visit the edges, where errors are largest.

evaluate.q: What would make the parity plot a more convincing validation?
evaluate.hint: Held-out points chosen to cover the corners, an error histogram, R squared or RMSE, and the counts of points.

create: Redraw the plot with a residual panel below it (error in percent against the estimate) and the count of training and testing points in the legend.
Design a check that the surrogate remains valid near the optimizer's final solution, which was not part of the original sample.

checks.q: What does a point exactly on the diagonal mean?
checks.hint: The two axes are the same quantity.
checks.answer: The response-surface estimate equals the direct simulation at that parameter set: zero error.

checks.q: How many coefficients has a full quadratic in 4 inputs?
Test dots scatter much more than training circles. Interpretation?
checks.answer: Overfitting: the surface follows the training data more closely than the underlying response. Remedies are fewer terms, more training runs or regularization.

checks.q: The maximum error is 0.8 percent. Is that enough?
checks.answer: It depends on the experimental uncertainty and on what the optimizer needs. If the target data have 10 percent uncertainty, 0.8 percent is negligible; if the optimizer must discriminate between candidates differing by 0.5 percent it is not.

checks.q: How would you reduce the inputs to build a cheaper surface?
checks.answer: Rank the parameters by a first-order sensitivity measure, keep those above a threshold, and refit; then compare the parity plot against the full fit.
